entities.summary:
Matthew of Cracow (German: Matthäus von Krakau), who died on March 14, 1410, was a profoundly influential German-Polish theologian, philosopher, and academic during the tumultuous era of the Western Schism. Rising from a humble background in Silesia, he became a distinguished professor at the University of Prague and later the first rector of the University of Heidelberg, eventually serving as Bishop of Worms. His intellectual contributions, particularly his incisive critiques of papal absolutism and advocacy for conciliar reform, positioned him as a pivotal voice in the late medieval struggle to redefine ecclesiastical authority, directly preceding the Council of Constance and the Hussite Wars.

Educated at the University of Prague, Matthew distinguished himself in theology and philosophy, contributing to the intellectual ferment that characterized Central European universities. His academic career culminated in 1386 with his election as the inaugural rector of the newly founded University of Heidelberg, a position he held twice, shaping its early scholastic traditions. Appointed Bishop of Worms in 1405 by Pope Innocent VII, he continued to serve as an advisor to King Ruprecht of Germany. His most significant work, "De modo uniendi et reformandi ecclesiam in concilio universali" (On the Method of Uniting and Reforming the Church in a Universal Council), written around 1406–1408, systematically argued for the superiority of a general council over the pope, advocating for radical structural reform to address the schism and pervasive corruption within the Church.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Matthew of Cracow's foundational writings on conciliarism profoundly influenced the intellectual trajectory of the Church reform movement, providing critical arguments that shaped the Council of Constance and its attempts to resolve the Western Schism. His work directly contributed to the theological debates that challenged papal supremacy and laid groundwork for future religious reforms.
